newsitem.title: USA: Clinton-Yeltsin summit tops US-Russia talks agenda.
newsitem.headline: Clinton-Yeltsin summit tops US-Russia talks agenda.

text.p: The upcoming summit between President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin topped the agenda in meetings on Thursday between Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Even before the discussions began, Chernomyrdin told reporters the summit would be held as expected in March, probably in the second half of the month.

There had been some question that Yeltsin, who underwent heart surgery in November and was diagnosed with pneumonia in January, was not well enough to attend such a meeting so soon. But at the White House on Thursday, a U.S. official gave a positive assessment of Yeltsin's fitness.
"He (Yeltsin) is running the show and is on top of his brief," the official said, requesting anonymity. "We are encouraged by what we're hearing."

For his part, Chernomyrdin called the March summit "a very important meeting" and said discussions with Gore were aimed at preparing the U.S. and Russian presidents for the meeting, their first since last April's summit in Moscow.
Although it is the U.S. turn to host the summit, U.S. officials mentioned the possibility of holding the March meeting in a third country closer to Russia in deference to Yeltsin's health.

Gore and Chernomyrdin have been meeting roughly every six months for the last four years in a series of get-togethers also including an array of government ministers aimed at dismantling Cold War barriers.
The meetings, which have become the key diplomatic channel between Washington and Moscow, will continue on Friday, when Chernomyrdin will also meet Clinton.

Russian anxiety about NATO expansion into central Europe will be a dominant theme. Chernomyrdin has said publicly that if NATO extends membership to Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic as expected at its July meeting, it could undermine Yeltsin's government and encourage ultranationalists.
U.S. officials have been working to allay such fears, but Chernomyrdin's concerns were evident to members of Congress who met with him earlier Thursday.

"We talked about the tremendous progress Russia has made towards a more democratic and market society, the opportunity for investment and growth and the need to manage our relations, including NATO, in a way that strengthens Russian democracy and does not weaken Russian democracy," House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said.

Besides NATO, Gore and Chernomyrdin will discuss progress on the international space station -- questions about Russian financing for the project have caused jitters in Washington -- and increased foreign investment in Russia.
Foreign investment is now roughly $9 billion, with U.S. investors representing $3 billion of that, a second U.S. official said.
"We strongly believe that figure can increase very, very dramatically if certain steps are taken by the Russian Federation," the official said, requesting anonymity.

The official said Russia needs to undertake three basic reforms to encourage more U.S. private investment: ratify a bilateral investment treaty, enact two oil production sharing amendments and reform its tax system.

Of the oil amendments, the official said: "These two amendments, if passed, would make it possible for our energy companies to proceed with investments in Russia which would be well in excess of $50 billion ... (over) 10-50 years."
Gore and Chernomyrdin will travel to Chicago on Saturday for a meeting with U.S. and Russian business leaders.
